## The specification menu {#the-specification-menu .smaller}

```{r}
#| label: menu-table
#| output: asis
# The eleven decisions of the menu (data/menu_options.csv), with the options
# that the curve keeps and the others grouped by the judgement of the course.
judgement_txt <- c(other_question = "another question", weaker_answer = "a weaker answer",
                   check = "a check", unavailable = "not in the public file")
level_txt <- c(estimand = "1 – Estimands", measurement = "2 – Measurement",
               estimation = "3 – Estimation")
off_txt <- menu_opts |>
  dplyr::filter(!on_curve) |>
  dplyr::summarise(txt = paste0(paste(label, collapse = ", "), " *(", judgement_txt[dplyr::first(judgement)], ")*"),
            .by = c(axis, judgement)) |>
  dplyr::summarise(off = paste(txt, collapse = "; "), .by = axis)
menu_rows <- menu_opts |>
  dplyr::filter(on_curve) |>
  dplyr::summarise(level = dplyr::first(level), decision = dplyr::first(decision),
            on = paste(label, collapse = "; "), .by = axis) |>
  dplyr::left_join(off_txt, by = "axis") |>
  dplyr::mutate(off = dplyr::coalesce(off, "–"),
         level = dplyr::if_else(level == dplyr::lag(level, default = ""), "", level_txt[level]),
         line = paste0("| ", level, " | **", decision, "** | ", on, " | ", off, " |"))
cat(c("::: {.fs-55}", # r-style: keep – writes the Markdown of the table
      "| Level | Decision | On the curve | Off the curve |",
      "|:--|:--|:--|:--|",
      menu_rows$line, ":::"), sep = "\n")
```

::: {.small}
Five decisions keep more than one option, and they cross into the **`r nrow(curve)`** specifications of the curve. The [decision map](../cases/housing/map.html) gives the reason for every option.
:::

::: notes
Here is the menu, and everything that follows is built on it. It is the full list of decisions that any analyst of this claim has to take, eleven of them, at three levels. Level 1 decides which question is asked: the outcome, the comparison group, which emails are counted, which names, and whose replies. Level 2 decides how the outcome is measured: what to do with the five replies whose greeting nobody coded, and with the emails that bounced. Level 3 decides how the answer is reached: the model, the covariates, the test and the scale of the result. Every option on the right was considered and left off the curve for a stated reason: it answers another question, it answers this one less well, it is a check, or it is simply not in the public file. The decision map on the site gives the reason for each.
:::

## The curve of 64 {#the-curve-of-64 .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **Comparison group** – white names, or white and Black names
- **Emails counted** – replies only, or all delivered emails
- **Replies without a greeting code** – left out, or counted as no greeting
- **Model** – a difference in proportions, or logistic regression
- **Adjustment** – none; hard-to-find address; place, without ethnic composition; or place, with ethnic composition
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 4 = **`r nrow(curve)`**. The reference specification is the raw gap of the paper: `r fmt_num(curve_ref$rate_hisp, 1)`% against `r fmt_num(curve_ref$rate_comp, 1)`%, **`r fmt_num(curve_ref$b_pp, 2)` points**, *t* = `r fmt_num(curve_ref$stat, 2)` on `r curve_ref$df` df, n = `r curve_ref$n` replies.

```{.r}
try_spec(comparison = "white", population = "replies", uncoded = "drop",
         model = "lpm", adjust = "none")
```
:::

::: notes
Five of the eleven decisions keep more than one option on the curve. The comparison, with white names or with white and Black names. The emails counted, replies or every delivered email. The five uncoded replies, left out or counted as replies without a greeting. The model, a difference in proportions or a logistic regression. And the adjustment, four sets of covariates from none to the set of the original model, in the thirds that the public file holds. [advance] Two times two times two times two times four is sixty-four specifications, and the course has fitted every one. The reference specification is the raw gap of the paper, Hispanic against white names among the replies, with no covariates: forty-one against sixty-one per cent, a gap of twenty points. In the helpers, every argument of try underscore spec defaults to that reference, so changing one thing means changing one argument.
:::

## Ground rules for the menu {#one-deviation-and-a-reason-for-it .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **Change one decision at a time**, and hold the others at the reference specification. When a result moves, you can then say what moved it
- **An option off the curve is refused** by `try_spec()`, with the reason from the menu and the page that teaches it. Asking for one is part of the exercise
- **One sign convention:** every estimate is Hispanic minus comparison names, in percentage points, so below zero is the direction of the claim
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The estimand statement on the [decision map](../cases/housing/map.html) rewrites itself as you choose. A change in its first sentence asks another question, a change inside its parentheses counts the outcome differently, and a change in the second sentence reaches the answer another way.
:::

::: notes
Three ground rules before you touch the menu. First, change one decision at a time and hold the others at the reference. That sounds restrictive, but it is what makes the class chart readable, because when a result sits somewhere surprising we can say what put it there. Second, if you ask for an option that is off the curve, try underscore spec refuses it, tells you why, and names the page that teaches it. Trying one is part of the exercise, because the refusal is where the reasoning lives. Third, one sign convention binds everybody: every estimate is the Hispanic names minus the comparison names, in percentage points, so below zero is the direction of the claim. [advance] And the decision map on the site shows the estimand statement rewriting itself as you choose, which tells you whether a choice changes the question or only the way of answering it.
:::
